title: The Nine Chambers (Aiq Bekar)
otherNames: the nine Chambers (J.F.'s 1651 English Agrippa, III.xxx, p. 442; verified in EEBO-TCP A26565)
Aiq Bekar / Aiq Beker / AIQ BKR, from the Hebrew mnemonic איק בכר (a later name: it does not occur anywhere in J.F.'s 1651 English, verified by a whole-text search; the 1533 Latin was not seen)
Ayak Bakar, Ayaq Bakhar (other spellings of the mnemonic; not checked against a named source)
Kabbalah (Qabalah) of the Nine Chambers (Golden Dawn-derived and popular usage, as the researcher recalls; not checked. It is not Agrippa's phrase in J.F. 1651, verified)
Cabalistic cipher of the nine chambers (descriptive)
family: A cipher-writing system, not an alphabet of new letters. The 27 Hebrew letters are grouped by numerical value into nine cells of a grid, and each letter is written as the lines that bound its cell plus one to three points. It is printed in the same chapter (III.30) as Agrippa's Celestial, Malachim and Transitus fluvii ('passing of the River') alphabets, after them (verified for the 1651 English, pp. 439-443). The Freemasons' ('pigpen') cipher, reported from the 18th century, uses the same mechanism; a descent from Agrippa is often asserted, but no document shows it.
summary: Agrippa prints this way of writing Hebrew letters as geometric signs in De occulta philosophia III.30 (complete edition, 1533; heading and wording verified in J.F.'s 1651 English) and gives it as 'another fashion amongst the Cabalists'. The 27 Hebrew letters (22 plus five finals) are sorted by value into nine 'Chambers' of a grid of four lines crossing at right angles: 1-10-100 in the first, 2-20-200 in the second, and so on to 9-90-900. A letter is written as the part of the grid that bounds its chamber, with one, two or three points for the first, second or third letter of the chamber (the unit, the ten or the hundred), and the figures of a name such as Michael can be contracted into a single character, in which, J.F. says, the points are usually left out. The Freemasons' ('pigpen') cipher works the same way, but no document traces the descent.

firstAttestation.notes: This is the earliest printing of the chamber-and-points script that can be named here. It is not evidence for the first record of the grouping itself: Agrippa gives the method to 'the Cabalists', and the mnemonic איק בכר is Hebrew, but no Jewish witness earlier than 1533 was found or checked. Agrippa sent a draft of the work to Trithemius, whose reply is dated 'From our Monastery of Peapolis, the 8. day of April, An. M. D. X.' (1651 front matter, verified), so the draft existed by 8 April 1510. It is reported to survive as Würzburg, Universitätsbibliothek, M. ch. q. 50 (sibling research; not seen). In 'To the Reader' Agrippa says that for the print 'we added some Chapters, and we inserted many things' (1651, verified), so the passage cannot be dated to the draft without the manuscript; Perrone Compagni's critical edition (Leiden: Brill, 1992) would settle it. Dates of 1531 in popular accounts probably confuse it with the 1531 printing of Book I alone (sibling research); Book I's dedication to Hermann von Wied, reprinted in the complete work, is dated 'From Mechlinia, Anno M. D. XXXI. In the moneth of January' (1651 front matter, verified).

claims.claim: In III.30 Agrippa divides the 27 Hebrew letters (22 plus five finals) into three classes of nine: units, tens and hundreds, the five finals counting 500-900. He then sets them in nine chambers of a grid, chamber n holding n, 10n and 100n.
claims.evidence: Verified in J.F. 1651, III.xxx (EEBO-TCP A26565). p. 441: 'The twenty seven Characters of the Hebrews may be divided into three Classes, whereof every one [two illegible words] l[..]ters'; the TCP keyers could not read the words after 'every one', so the researcher's recalled 'shall contain nine letters' cannot be confirmed and must not be quoted. The third class 'hath the other four letters, with the five final, by order'. p. 442: 'They do now and then distribute these three Classes into nine Chambers, whereof the first is of unites, viz. intellectual, celestial and elemental: The second is of Twos. The third of Threes, and so of the rest'. Agrippa's numeral table (II.xix, 1651 p. 232, verified) gives the finals ך 500, ם 600, ן 700, ף 800, ץ 900. The 1533 Latin was not seen.
sources: Agrippa, De occulta philosophia (1533), III.30 (not seen)
J.F. trans. 1651, III.xxx pp. 441-442 and II.xix p. 232 (EEBO-TCP A26565, verified)

claims.claim: Each letter is written as the figure of its chamber: the lines of the grid that bound that cell. One point marks the first letter of the chamber, two the second and three the third.
claims.evidence: Agrippa's own rule, verified in J.F. 1651, III.xxx, pp. 442-443: the Chambers 'are framed by the interfection [so the TCP keying; probably a misread long-s 'interſection'] of four paralell lines, intersecting themselves into right angles'; 'Out of which being dissected into parts, proceed nine particular figures'; these characterize their letter by points, 'which if itbe [sic, TCP] of one poynt shews the first letter of that Chamber; if of two, the second; if of three, the third letter'. The researcher's recalled wording ('if it be of the first note in its Chamber, it requires one point ...') does not occur and has been withdrawn. In each chamber the first, second and third letters are the unit, the ten and the hundred.

claims.claim: The three classes stand for three worlds. The units are intellectual things (the nine orders of angels), the tens celestial things (the nine orbs), and the hundreds inferior things (the four elements and five kinds of perfect compounds).
claims.evidence: This is Agrippa's assertion, reported as his doctrine, not as a fact about the letters. Verified in J.F. 1651, III.xxx, p. 441: the first class are 'the seals or marks of simple numbers, and of intellectuall things, distributed into nine orders of Angels'; the second hath 'the marks of tens, and of Celestial things, in the nine Orbs of the heavens'; the third letters are 'marks of hundreds, and inferior things, viz. four simple Elements, and of five kinds of perfect compounds'.

claims.claim: The method comes from Jewish Kabbalah ('the Cabalists').
claims.evidence: Agrippa ascribes it to the Cabalists. The heading reads 'Another manner of making Characters, delivered by Cabalists' (p. 439), and the passage opens 'There is moreover another fashion amongst the Cabalists, formerly had in great esteem, but now it is so common, that it is placed amongst prophane things' (p. 441; J.F. 1651, verified; the researcher's 'There is also ... once had in great esteem' was misworded). The grouping by unit value and the mnemonic איק בכר are Jewish letter-number lore (researcher's statement; no source named). No pre-1533 Jewish witness of the chamber-figures-with-points script was found or checked.

claims.claim: The names 'Aiq Bekar' and 'Kabbalah of the Nine Chambers' are Agrippa's.
claims.evidence: Verified for the 1651 English: J.F. speaks of 'nine Chambers' (p. 442), but a whole-text search of EEBO-TCP A26565 finds no 'Aiq', 'Beker' or 'Bekar', and no phrase such as 'Kabbalah (Cabala) of the Nine Chambers'. On that evidence the names are not Agrippa's in J.F.'s text. The 1533 Latin was not seen. The researcher attributes 'Qabalah of the Nine Chambers' to Golden Dawn-derived and popular literature; not checked.
sources: J.F. 1651, III.xxx p. 442 and whole text (EEBO-TCP A26565, verified)

claims.claim: Agrippa published the nine chambers in 1531.
claims.evidence: Popular accounts give 1531; the researcher recalls Wikipedia's 'Pigpen cipher' among them (not checked). Book III, which holds the chapter, was first printed in the complete edition of 1533 (colophon July 1533, rendered at the end of the 1651 English, p. 583, verified). The 1531 printings held Book I only (sibling research; their printers are recalled there, not verified). A possible source of the confusion, suggested by the fact-checker and not documented: Book I's dedication, reprinted in the complete work, is dated January 1531 (1651 front matter, verified). Use 1533.

claims.claim: The Freemasons' or 'pigpen' cipher descends from Agrippa's nine chambers.
claims.evidence: The two systems work the same way: a grid of two vertical and two horizontal lines is cut into nine cells, a letter is the set of lines bounding its cell, and dots separate letters that share a cell. Popular accounts state the descent. But no document is known that names Agrippa as the source of the Masonic cipher, and the steps between 1533 and the 1700s are unknown. The common modern pigpen key also uses X-shaped grids (as the researcher recalls Wikipedia; not checked), while Agrippa's text describes only the four-line grid (1651, p. 442, verified). Present this as a likely debt, not a proven one.

claims.claim: Freemasons used a grid-and-dot cipher for the Latin alphabet in the 18th century.
claims.evidence: Reported, not seen: a printed 'alphabet des Francs-Maçons' in the 1745 exposure attributed to Pérau, and the 1794 gravestone of James Leeson in Trinity Churchyard, New York (both as the researcher recalls them). Neither witness was seen by the research or by the fact-check, so the standing is lowered from 'documented' to 'attributed' until one is verified.

claims.claim: The Rosicrucians used the cipher, hence 'Rosicrucian cipher'.
claims.evidence: The name is current in popular cryptography for a one-grid variant with several letters per cell, told apart by dots (researcher's recollection; not checked). No early Rosicrucian document using it is known to the researcher or the fact-checker, and the researcher knows of none in the manifestos of 1614-1616 (not checked). Report the name, not the use.
'Napoleon cipher' is a popular alternative name for the pigpen (as the researcher recalls Wikipedia; not checked). No evidence is known that Napoleon used it.

claims.claim: Prisoners and soldiers used the pigpen in the American Civil War.
claims.evidence: Reported in popular cryptographic histories; the researcher associates it with Kahn (1967), but the passage and page were not checked by the research or the fact-check.

claims.claim: The nine chambers were used to reduce letter values so that names could be traced as sigils on Agrippa's planetary squares (II.22).
claims.evidence: This is the explanation in Golden Dawn teaching and in modern commentary (Tyson 1993, as recalled; neither checked). Agrippa does not mention the planetary tables in III.30 (1651, verified). In II.xxii ('Of the tables of the Planets ...', 1651 p. 239, verified) he says the seals and characters are drawn from the tables but leaves the method to the reader: 'Now how the seals, and Characters of the Stars, and spirits are drawn from these tables, the wise searcher, and he which shall understand the verifying of these tables, shall easily find out' (J.F. 1651, p. 242, verified). The reduction itself is arithmetic: every letter in a chamber reduces to the same unit.
sources: J.F. 1651, II.xxii pp. 239, 242 and III.xxx (EEBO-TCP A26565, verified)
Tyson (ed.), Three Books of Occult Philosophy (1993) (not checked)

lettersSource: 27 entries, one per Hebrew letter, in Agrippa's class order: the nine units Aleph-Teth, the nine tens Yod-Tsade, then Qoph, Resh, Shin, Tav and the five finals as hundreds (class order and final values verified in J.F. 1651, III.xxx p. 441 and II.xix p. 232). The extra key 'chambers' gives the nine cells, each with its three letters, its mnemonic (איק בכר גלש דמת הנך וסם זען חפף טצץ; arithmetic checked), the sides drawn and a suggested path (checked against the sides). NO FORM WAS TRACED. Neither the 1533 woodcut nor the 1651 cut was seen (EEBO-TCP keys the figures only as blank figure blocks). Each figure is deduced from Agrippa's verbal rule: Chambers 'framed by the interfection of four paralell lines, intersecting themselves into right angles', 'dissected into parts' into 'nine particular figures', plus one, two or three points (1651, p. 442, verified). The text does not give the layout ('as is expressed in this following figure'). The grid is ASSUMED to run in Hebrew order, row by row from the top right (chamber 1 top right, chamber 9 bottom left), the layout of the modern charts as the researcher and the fact-checker recall them. If the 1533 grid runs in rows from the top left, chambers 1/3, 4/6 and 7/9 swap figures and 2, 5, 8 stay. If it runs in columns from the top right, 1, 5 and 9 keep their figures and the rest change; in columns from the top left, only 5 is safe. One look at the figure settles all of it. The placement of the points is the site's own. Trace the grid, the nine figures and the Michael figures from III.30 in a 1533 copy, or check them against the 1651 cut (pp. 442-443, EEBO page image tcp:52070:237). Direction for the page: keyed to Hebrew, rtl.

uses.use: Making the 'character' (seal) of an angel's name: write each letter as its chamber figure, then run the figures together.
uses.evidence: Agrippa's worked example in III.30 is Michael (מיכאל). Verified in J.F. 1651, p. 443: 'as if thou wouldest frame the Character Michael [Hebrew], that comes forth thus, extended with five figures'; 'Which then are contracted to three figures, after this manner'; 'Which then are contracted into one, yet the points Notariacon are wont to be omitted, and then there comes forth such a Character of Michael.' (The researcher's recalled 'into one, yet more abbreviated' and 'all these are called by the name of Michael' do not occur and are withdrawn.) Under the assumed layout the five figures are: Mem, the [ bracket with two points; Yod, the L with two points; Kaph, the cup with two points; Aleph, the L with one point; Lamed, the reversed L with two points. The three-figure and one-figure forms cannot be worked out from the text and must be traced; the one-figure form carries no points. The chapter closes by saying that such characters do not compel angels: we 'devote and consecrate to them figures, and marks, by which we cannot any way compel them to us, but by which we rise up to them' (J.F. 1651, p. 444, verified).

uses.use: Reducing a name's numbers to units (gematria by chambers).
uses.evidence: All the letters in one chamber share a unit (Aleph, Yod and Qoph all reduce to 1, and so on). Later occultists used this to fit names onto the 3x3 to 9x9 planetary squares when tracing sigils (Golden Dawn; Tyson 1993; as recalled, not checked). Agrippa's III.30 does not describe this use (verified for 1651); in II.xxii he leaves the method of drawing the seals from the tables to 'the wise searcher' (J.F. 1651, p. 242, verified).

uses.use: Secret writing of the Latin alphabet: the Freemasons' or 'pigpen' cipher and its variants.
uses.evidence: The same grid-and-dot mechanism is reported for Latin letters from the 18th century on: Masonic exposures and gravestones, then popular puzzle books (none seen). The grid's direction is unverified. Six of the nine figures (chambers 1, 3, 4, 6, 7 and 9) depend on whether the 1533 grid runs from the right, as assumed here, or from the left. Check the woodcut before drawing, or label the drawing as a diagram of the rule.

Agrippa's text does not give the layout of the grid ('as is expressed in this following figure', 1651 p. 442, verified). Rows are assumed. In columns from the top right, chambers 1, 5 and 9 keep their figures and the rest change; in columns from the top left, only chamber 5 is safe.
The number and arrangement of the points as printed (in a row, a triangle or a column) were not seen. The level row used here is the site's own.

Do not write 'Agrippa invented' this cipher. He ascribes it to the Cabalists. Do not write 'the Rosicrucians used it' or 'Napoleon used it'. Do not present the pigpen's descent from Agrippa as documented.
The fully contracted Michael character has no points ('the points Notariacon are wont to be omitted', 1651 p. 443). Do not add points to it.

Numeric values: in this system the finals are 500-900. If the site computes numeric from hebrew.js and that file gives finals their ordinary values (20, 40, 50, 80, 90), the page will be wrong for the finals. Show the system's values and say so.

The transliterator: the system writes Hebrew letters, not Latin ones. A Latin-to-Hebrew step would be the site's own and must be labelled as such. The contracted forms (several letters merged into one character) cannot be generated by rule from the text.

Living organisations: the Masonic cipher and Golden Dawn teaching circulate in living orders. Give a generic Latin key as a cryptographic illustration if wanted. Do not reproduce Masonic emblems, ritual texts or Golden Dawn papers. Describe the Leeson gravestone; do not reproduce it.

Quotations are J.F. 1651 (public domain), verified against EEBO-TCP A26565; two readings ('interfection', 'itbe ... poynt') should be checked against the page image before printing.
